cards.title: What Is an Aggregate?
cards.teaser: An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects — entities and value objects — treated as a single unit for the purpose of data changes. It has a clear boundary, a designated root, and one consistency rule: the whole cluster must always satisfy its invariants.

runs.text: Eric Evans introduced the aggregate pattern in
(2003) to address a deceptively simple problem: in a domain model with dozens of interrelated objects, how do you know what belongs together and what rules must hold at all times?

The answer is the aggregate: a consistency boundary drawn around a set of objects. Within that boundary, all objects obey a shared set of invariants, and changes to any object in the cluster are made as an atomic unit.

runs.text: The key insight is that the aggregate boundary is a
, not just an ownership boundary. Everything inside must always satisfy the aggregate's invariants. Everything outside is a separate concern.

An aggregate is a cluster of objects that live together because they have rules that involve each other. You talk to the cluster through one designated door — the root — and the cluster guarantees it always stays in a valid state.

cards.title: The Aggregate Root
cards.teaser: The aggregate root is the single entity in an aggregate that the outside world is allowed to reference. All commands enter through the root; all invariants are enforced by the root. External objects hold the root's identity, never an interior object's reference.

runs.text: Evans's rule is explicit: "external objects can hold references to the root only." This is not a suggestion — it is the structural guarantee that makes an aggregate's consistency boundary meaningful.

items.text: No code outside the aggregate modifies an interior entity directly. All changes flow through methods on the root.
After any internal mutation, the root checks that all invariants still hold. If they do not, it raises a domain exception.
The root's identity (its ID) is the identity of the aggregate. A reference to the aggregate is a reference to its root's ID.

runs.text: A practical consequence: if you find yourself injecting an inner entity (e.g.,
) into a service and calling methods on it without going through
, you have violated the aggregate boundary. The fix is to move that operation to a method on the root.

Leaking inner entity references to callers is the most common aggregate violation. Once an outer object holds a direct reference to an OrderLine, nothing prevents it from mutating that line in ways that break Order-level invariants.
The aggregate root is the bouncer. Every command must go through it, and it decides whether the operation is allowed. Nobody bypasses it to talk directly to the people inside.

cards.title: Invariant Enforcement
cards.teaser: An invariant is a rule that must always hold within the aggregate. The aggregate root enforces all invariants atomically — after any operation, before control leaves the boundary, every invariant must be satisfied or the operation is rejected.

runs.text: Invariants are the reason aggregates exist. Without them, you would have no principled way to decide what belongs together in a single cluster.

aggregate with two invariants: (1) total line quantity cannot exceed the warehouse allocation, and (2) an order cannot be confirmed if it has no lines. These are checked by the root on every mutation:
does not check the allocation — it cannot, because it does not know about sibling lines. Only
has the full picture. This is the essential value of the aggregate root as invariant enforcer: it holds all the state needed to evaluate cross-entity rules.

An invariant check that cannot be implemented inside a single aggregate is a signal that you may have drawn the aggregate boundary in the wrong place — or that the invariant is cross-aggregate, which means eventual consistency is the appropriate tool.
An invariant is a promise the aggregate makes about itself — like "I will never have more items than my allocation." The root checks that promise every time anything changes inside.

cards.title: One Aggregate Per Transaction
cards.teaser: Modify exactly one aggregate per transaction. This rule is not a performance hint — it is the structural guarantee that aggregates are self-contained consistency units. Crossing the boundary in a single transaction couples two aggregates and erodes both.

runs.text: Vaughn Vernon, in his three-part series
(DDDCQRS, 2012), states this as Rule 2: "Modify one aggregate instance per transaction." It is the most frequently broken rule in aggregate design and the most important one to follow.

Why? Aggregates are consistency boundaries. If a single transaction spans two aggregates, you are effectively merging them — their invariants now depend on each other's state within that transaction. You have undermined the decomposition.

items.text: in the same transaction couples their lifecycle. If the inventory update fails, the database rollback undoes the order change — but business rules about partial failures are now hidden inside transaction atomicity.
aggregate reacts in a separate transaction, possibly with retry and compensation logic.

runs.text: When teams first encounter this rule, the typical objection is: "but I need both to succeed or both to fail." That objection is valid — but the answer is not to merge them into one transaction. The answer is to design the saga or process manager that provides the compensation when one succeeds and the other fails.

If you find yourself frequently needing to update two aggregates in one transaction, question whether they are really two aggregates or whether they should be one. But be cautious — the reflex is usually to merge; the correct move is usually to design the eventual consistency.

One transaction, one aggregate. If you need to change two aggregates "together," you are really changing them in sequence with compensation if the second fails — not atomically. Aggregates are the atoms of consistency.

cards.title: Cross-Aggregate Consistency Is Eventual
cards.teaser: Between aggregates, you cannot have transactional consistency — and you should not want it. Cross-aggregate consistency is achieved eventually, via domain events, sagas, or process managers. This is a feature, not a compromise.

items.text: When an aggregate changes state, it raises a domain event. Other aggregates (or projections) subscribe to that event and update in separate transactions. Example:
aggregate handles it and decrements stock.
For multi-step flows spanning several aggregates, a saga orchestrates the sequence and handles compensation. The saga itself is often an aggregate with its own state machine.

runs.text: Eventual consistency between aggregates is not just an architectural concession — it often reflects reality more faithfully. In the physical world, a warehouse decrement and an order confirmation do not happen instantaneously together. Modelling them as eventual makes the model honest about failure modes.

The practical question is: how long is "eventual"? For most domain events processed by a message bus with retries, consistency lag is milliseconds to seconds. For sagas involving external systems, it may be minutes. The business must accept that window — and in most domains, it already does.

Vernon's Rule 4 states: "Use eventual consistency outside the aggregate boundary." This is not a distributed systems concern — it applies even in a single-process monolith. The aggregate boundary is the unit of transactional commitment regardless of deployment topology.

Two aggregates cannot be updated in the same transaction. Instead, one changes first and publishes an event; the other reacts in a later transaction. "Both succeed or both fail" becomes "one succeeds, then compensates if the other fails."

cards.title: Reference by Identity
cards.teaser: Aggregates reference each other by identity — by holding an ID, not an object reference. This keeps aggregate boundaries hard, prevents lazy-loading leaks across boundaries, and makes the dependency direction explicit.

An ID signals to the reader that this is a cross-aggregate reference. An object reference obscures whether you are looking at an owned entity or a referenced aggregate.
IDs serialize trivially. Object graphs do not.

An aggregate refers to another aggregate using only its ID — like a database foreign key, not an object pointer. This prevents one aggregate from accidentally reading or changing another aggregate's internal state.

cards.title: Aggregate Size — Small Wins
cards.teaser: Smaller aggregates are better. They are easier to load, cheaper to lock, simpler to understand, and less likely to produce contention. Vernon's "Effective Aggregate Design" rule of thumb: if you feel the aggregate growing, that is a signal to split it.

runs.text: series dedicates significant attention to aggregate size. His central argument: the natural instinct to build large aggregates is wrong. Large aggregates produce:

items.text: A large aggregate is locked for the duration of a transaction. The more objects inside, the more concurrent operations compete for that lock. High-traffic systems with large aggregates produce deadlocks and timeouts.
Loading a large aggregate forces the entire object graph into memory even when the operation only touches one part of it.
Large aggregates accumulate many invariants, some of which may conflict or be difficult to reason about together.
A large aggregate requires a large setup in tests. Small aggregates are dramatically easier to unit test in isolation.

runs.text: Vernon's practical rules for aggregate size:

items.text: Model true invariants in the aggregate.
Only include objects whose consistency with each other must be guaranteed atomically.
Start with just the root and the minimum supporting objects. Add more only when an invariant demands it.
Do not include objects just because they are related — include them only because they participate in an invariant.
If consistency between objects can be eventual, they belong in separate aggregates.

runs.text: Keep aggregates as small as possible. The question to ask for every object: "does this object need to change atomically with the root, because a rule spans both?" If no, it belongs outside.

cards.title: Repository Per Aggregate Root
cards.teaser: Each aggregate root gets exactly one repository. The repository is the persistence boundary — it loads and saves the entire aggregate as a unit. No repository is created for interior entities; they have no meaningful existence outside their aggregate.

runs.text: The repository pattern in DDD has a one-to-one relationship with aggregate roots. A repository exists to reconstitute and persist an aggregate as a whole. This correspondence is not incidental — it enforces the aggregate's consistency boundary at the persistence layer.

A repository for an interior entity is a design smell. It signals either that the entity's aggregate boundary was drawn incorrectly, or that the entity has been confused with an aggregate root.

In practice, some teams add finder methods to repositories (e.g., find_by_customer_id). This is acceptable as long as finders return complete, valid aggregates — not partial projections. Projections are the domain of query models, not repositories.
One repository, one aggregate root. The repository loads and saves the whole aggregate at once. Never create a repository for an object that lives inside an aggregate — it has no meaning on its own.

cards.title: Loading the Aggregate
cards.teaser: When loading an aggregate, you have two choices: load the entire object graph eagerly or load lazily. For aggregates, the answer is almost always eager. Lazy loading inside an aggregate boundary is a trap that leads to ghost invariant violations.

runs.text: The loading question is orthogonal to aggregate design but deeply practical. The aggregate pattern assumes the root has access to all interior objects when evaluating invariants. Lazy loading breaks this assumption silently.
with an invariant: total quantity across all lines cannot exceed the warehouse allocation. If
is called in a context where the session is closed, the invariant check runs against an empty list — and silently passes.

items.text: The aggregate is fully materialized when the repository returns it. All invariant checks have complete data.
ORM proxies can silently return empty collections outside a session, causing invariant checks to run against partial state.
The performance concern is real but solvable.
If loading the full aggregate is expensive, the solution is to keep aggregates smaller — not to add lazy loading. Vernon makes this explicit in Effective Aggregate Design Part II.

runs.text: For read-heavy use cases, the solution is a separate query model (CQRS read side) — not a lazily loaded aggregate. The aggregate is the write model; load it fully when you need to change it.

ORMs like SQLAlchemy and Hibernate default to lazy loading on relationships. When using these tools with aggregates, explicitly configure eager loading for all interior collections to avoid invariant violations caused by session-closed lazy loads.

Always load the entire aggregate before changing it. If you allow lazy loading, you risk enforcing invariants against a half-loaded object — which means the invariant check lies. Load it all upfront; split the aggregate if that is too expensive.

cards.title: Invariant Types — A Taxonomy
cards.teaser: Not all invariants are the same. A four-level taxonomy distinguishes single-attribute invariants (trivial) from cross-aggregate invariants (the hard ones requiring eventual consistency). Knowing the type tells you where to enforce it.

runs.text: Understanding the type of an invariant determines both where it can be enforced and what consistency guarantee is required. There are four levels:

items.text: A rule on one field of one entity. Example: order quantity must be positive. Enforced in the value object or entity constructor. No aggregate coordination needed.
A rule spanning multiple fields of the same entity. Example: discount percentage cannot exceed the margin percentage. Enforced by the entity's method or the root when updating both fields.

A rule that spans multiple entities inside the same aggregate. Example: the sum of all line quantities must not exceed the order allocation. Enforced by the aggregate root after any mutation to interior entities. This is the core use case for aggregates.

A rule that spans two or more aggregates. Example: total inventory deducted across all orders cannot exceed warehouse stock. This cannot be enforced transactionally. It is enforced eventually, via domain events or periodic reconciliation, with compensating actions for violations.

runs.text: The cross-aggregate invariant is the hardest. The common mistake is to respond to it by enlarging the aggregate to include both sides. Vernon's advice: resist that reflex. Ask whether the business actually requires strict atomicity for this rule, or whether eventual consistency is acceptable. In most domains, it is.

A useful litmus test for cross-aggregate invariants: ask the domain expert what happens if the invariant is temporarily violated and then corrected. If the answer is "we send a notice and correct it," eventual consistency is the correct model. If the answer is "that can never happen," you may need to reconsider the aggregate boundary.

Invariants come in four strengths: rules on one field, rules between fields of one entity, rules that span entities inside an aggregate, and rules that span different aggregates. The aggregate boundary is drawn to enclose the third type. The fourth type is handled eventually.

cards.title: Designing Aggregate Boundaries
cards.teaser: Aggregate boundary design is an iterative process, not a schema migration. Start with the smallest possible aggregate: root plus value objects. Grow it only when an invariant demands it. Shrink it whenever you find a cluster that never changes together.

runs.text: Vernon's three-part series frames aggregate boundary design as a discovery process driven by invariants, not by data relationships. The steps:

items.text: Before drawing any boundary, list all the business rules that must hold atomically. Invariants, not object graphs, define where the boundary goes.
Begin with the root entity alone (plus necessary value objects). Ask: which other objects are strictly required to enforce these invariants? Include only those.
Simulate concurrent updates. Do multiple use cases try to update the same aggregate simultaneously? Contention is a signal to split.
If two sub-clusters of the aggregate never appear in the same invariant together, they may belong in separate aggregates connected by eventual consistency.
Aggregates are a modeling tool, not a technical artifact. Domain experts understand which changes must be atomic. Ask them explicitly.

runs.text: A common discovery trigger: you notice that loading an aggregate is slow because it pulls in thousands of records. This is almost always a sign that the aggregate is too large and contains collections that do not truly participate in invariants — they are query concerns, not command concerns.

Vernon proposes a concrete heuristic: if a collection inside an aggregate can grow unboundedly (e.g., all comments on a post), it almost certainly does not belong inside the aggregate. Collections that participate in invariants are usually bounded and small.

Design aggregate boundaries by asking one question: which objects must change together because a business rule spans them? Start with just those objects. If you find the aggregate growing, ask whether the new objects genuinely participate in an invariant, or whether they just seemed related.

cards.title: Aggregate vs Entity Confusion
cards.teaser: An aggregate root IS an entity — but not every entity is an aggregate root. Entities can live inside an aggregate without being accessible from outside it. Confusing entity identity with aggregate root status leads to leaked boundaries and redundant repositories.

runs.text: This is one of the most frequent conceptual errors in DDD codebases. The confusion arises because both entities and aggregate roots have identity. But aggregate roots have an additional property: they are the external face of a consistency cluster.

The presence of a database foreign key does NOT imply a repository is needed. Foreign keys express relational structure; repositories express aggregate boundaries. These are different concerns.

An aggregate root is always an entity, but an entity is not always an aggregate root. The difference is whether the outside world is allowed to address it directly. Interior entities have IDs for internal tracking but cannot be fetched or changed from outside the aggregate.

cards.title: Aggregate Antipatterns
cards.teaser: Three aggregate antipatterns recur across codebases: the God Aggregate (too large), the Anemic Aggregate (no invariants), and the Transactionless Aggregate (multiple aggregates in one transaction). Each signals a different design error.

runs.text: Understanding the failure modes helps diagnose existing codebases and avoid repeating common errors.

items.text: One aggregate grows to contain dozens of entities and hundreds of invariants. Symptoms: loading it requires joining 20 tables; concurrent operations produce constant lock timeouts; adding a new invariant requires understanding the entire cluster. Cause: grouping by data proximity rather than by invariant. Remedy: decompose by asking which sub-clusters form their own invariant sets.

The aggregate has a root and some entities, but no invariants are enforced inside. All domain logic lives in services that manipulate the aggregate's internals directly. This is the anemic domain model applied at the aggregate level. The aggregate exists in name only — it provides no consistency guarantee. Remedy: move invariant checks into the root; ban direct mutation of interior entities from outside.

Multiple aggregates are always updated in the same transaction, violating the one-aggregate-per-transaction rule. Often rationalized as "we need atomicity." Symptoms: application services begin multiple transactions or create savepoints around multiple aggregate saves. Remedy: identify which aggregate owns the primary change; publish events; let the secondary aggregate react.

runs.text: A fourth antipattern worth naming: the
(violating reference-by-identity). This is often introduced by ORM bidirectional relationships. The fix is to remove the reverse navigation property and hold only an ID.

Anemic aggregates are the hardest to detect because the code compiles and tests pass. The invariants just are not enforced anywhere — they are comments in a design document, not executable rules. If your aggregate root has only getters and setters, it is anemic.

The three aggregate traps: too big (God Aggregate — contains everything), too hollow (Anemic Aggregate — contains no logic), and too coupled (Transactionless Aggregate — always saved with others). Each one tells you a different thing went wrong in the design.

cards.title: Aggregates in Practice — A Worked Example
cards.teaser: Applying all thirteen concepts to a single domain model — an e-commerce order — makes the abstract rules concrete. The exercise reveals how invariant identification drives boundary placement and how small, focused aggregates produce a design that is easy to test and maintain.
